messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

# Rajesh

Rajesh was forty-eight when his son Arjun fell ill. The boy had complained of a persistent fever one Tuesday morning in March, and by Thursday he was in the pediatric intensive care unit at Mount Sinai, his small body threaded with lines, his breathing labored. Rajesh remembered the smell—that acrid, chemical hospital smell that seemed to coat the back of his throat—and the sound of the monitors, their rhythmic beeping a metronome for his terror. For six weeks, Rajesh slept in a vinyl chair beside his son's bed. He did not sleep well. He would wake at three in the morning, certain that Arjun's oxygen saturation was dropping, and he would lean over the mattress to watch his son's chest rise and fall. The doctors said it was viral meningitis. They said the next seventy-two hours were critical. Rajesh had never prayed so hard in his life.

Arjun recovered. By May, he was home, his energy slowly returning, his appetite normalizing. The crisis passed. But something in Rajesh did not return with his son. Two years later, now fifty, he found himself unable to sleep when his wife traveled for work. The thought of being alone in the dark—of being unreachable, unprepared—would seize him around eight o'clock in the evening. He had come to believe that if he was not vigilant, if he allowed himself to relax into sleep in an unfamiliar place or without his wife nearby, disaster would strike again. It was irrational, he knew this, but the belief had taken root so deeply that he could not excavate it.

When Rajesh found himself facing a routine colonoscopy at his primary care physician's insistence, the old panic returned with vicious clarity. The appointment itself triggered a spiral: the thought of lying prone, of being sedated and therefore unable to monitor what was happening to his body, sent him into a state of hypervigilance that lasted days. To manage the dread, he began to mentally rehearse every possible complication—perforation, infection, anesthesia complications—running through each scenario in his mind as though he could inoculate himself against disaster by imagining it first. If he could anticipate the worst, he reasoned, he would not be blindsided. He would be prepared. The rehearsal gave him a momentary sense of control, a brief reprieve from the suffocating helplessness that had defined those weeks in the hospital. But the relief never lasted. Each time he cycled through the scenarios, the anxiety only deepened, and new catastrophes would suggest themselves—what if the doctor missed something? What if the sedation didn't wear off properly? What if, what if, what if? The rehearsal itself had become a source of dread; each imagined catastrophe, once conjured, lingered in his mind as a plausible threat, and he found himself hyperaware of any bodily sensation that might confirm his fears. The strategies meant to contain his anxiety had instead expanded the landscape of things he needed to worry about.

His wife, Priya, had begun to notice that Rajesh was asking her constantly for reassurance. Is it normal to feel this way before a procedure? Am I going to be okay? What if something goes wrong? The questions came in clusters, especially in the evenings, and no matter how many times Priya told him that millions of people underwent colonoscopies without incident, that the procedure was routine and safe, Rajesh would nod and seem to accept her words, only to circle back to the same fears an hour later. He was aware that his reassurance-seeking was exhausting her, that it had become a ritual neither of them could quite break. But without those moments of being told that he was safe, that he was okay, the anxiety felt like it might consume him entirely. Yet the reassurance itself had become a trigger—each time he asked Priya and received her answer, he would feel momentary relief, only to realize minutes later that he still did not truly believe her words, and the doubt would send him searching for new reassurances, new confirmations, as though the right combination of answers might finally make the fear stick.

The smell of antiseptic—even the faint chemical tang of his office's hand sanitizer—could now trigger the whole cycle anew. When his animation studio moved to a building adjacent to a medical plaza, Rajesh found himself hyperaware of every antiseptic scent that drifted through the ventilation system. His mind would immediately leap to the hospital, to Arjun's monitors, to his own helplessness. He would begin to catastrophize about his health, about his family's vulnerability, and he would reach for his phone to text Priya or to call his doctor's office with some new worry. The worst-case rehearsal would start up again, a familiar machinery grinding into motion, and Rajesh would sit at his desk unable to focus on his work, his hands trembling slightly as he tried to render movement on screen when his own body felt paralyzed by dread.

It was his supervisor's gentle concern—a note that his productivity had dropped significantly, that he seemed distracted and anxious—that finally prompted Rajesh to seek help. He was terrified that his mind was fracturing, that he was losing his grip on reality. What he feared most was that the hypervigilance that had once felt like protection would become permanent, that he would spend the rest of his life imprisoned by the fear that lightning would strike twice.

violation_explanations: The vignette describes maladaptive strategies (catastrophic rehearsal, reassurance-seeking) and triggers (antiseptic smells, colonoscopy appointment) but does not show that the maladaptive strategies themselves create or generate new triggers; instead, the narrative shows triggers activating strategies, not strategies creating triggers.
